analysis.one_liner: Gives Americans legal rights over the data companies collect on them and bans manipulative website design.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2020 by four Republican senators, the bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE DATA Act would create the first comprehensive federal privacy law. It would give people the right to see, correct, delete, and take with them the data companies hold; require explicit consent before companies process or share sensitive data like health, location, and biometric information; limit data collection to what a service actually needs; require big platforms to offer a version of their feeds that does not secretly use your browsing and location history; and ban 'dark patterns'—design tricks like autoplaying videos to keep children watching. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users—virtually every American—whose health, location, financial, and biometric data is currently bought, sold, and processed largely without meaningful consent. The bill also would protect children from interfaces designed to cultivate compulsive use, and give whistleblowers at data companies a voice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday internet users and their families

how_it_helps.text: Gives individuals the right to access, correct, delete, and port their covered data, free of charge twice a year, with companies responding within 90 days [S3].

Requires affirmative express consent before a company processes or transfers sensitive data—Social Security numbers, health information, financial accounts, biometrics, precise location, private messages—and lets parents consent for 13-to-16-year-olds before their data is sold [S3].
Bars companies from collecting, processing, or retaining more data than is reasonably necessary to provide the service, and from denying service to people who exercise their privacy rights [S3].
Requires platforms using 'opaque algorithms' to tell users and offer a one-click switch to a version that ranks content without using users' browsing history, location, and inferences [S3].

Prohibits large online operators from manipulating user interfaces to subvert user choice, running behavioral experiments on users without informed consent, or using features like video autoplay to cultivate compulsive usage by children under 13 [S3].
Establishes a Victims Relief Fund holding civil penalties for compensation to people harmed by violations, and authorizes $100 million for FTC enforcement; state attorneys general can also sue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large technology platforms, data brokers, and the online advertising industry, which would bear the cost of compliance—consent systems, data minimization, security programs, privacy officers, algorithm transparency, and exposure to FTC and state enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: Employee data is excluded from the bill's protections, so workers get no rights over the data their own employers collect on the job [S3].
Companies may offer different pricing based on whether a customer exercises privacy rights, which allows pay-for-privacy schemes that pressure lower-income users into giving up their data [S3].
The data broker section is modest: a $100 annual registration fee and civil penalties capped at $10,000 per year for failing to register [S3].
The bill relies heavily on FTC rulemaking that would take years—the act takes effect 18 months after enactment, with several required studies and rules due one to five years later [S3].

It includes a section governing the relationship between federal and state law; in comprehensive privacy bills, such provisions are typically contested because they can override stronger state privacy protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the average American, the benefits are substantial: a federal privacy floor does not currently exist, and this bill would create real rights to control sensitive personal data plus limits on manipulative design. The drawbacks are real but secondary—the employee-data carve-out, pay-for-privacy pricing, and light data broker penalties show the bill was written with an eye to business burden. Even a supporter would concede it is weaker than the strictest state laws in some respects; the honest comparison is against the status quo, where no federal privacy rights exist at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, no vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Wicker introduced the bill on September 17, 2020, joined by Republican Sens. Thune, Blackburn, and Fischer [S1].
All three cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day—its only action of the Congress [S5].
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action was ever recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large technology platforms, data brokers, and the online advertising industry are better off, because they avoided a comprehensive federal privacy law and kept the status quo, in which no federal law gives consumers rights over their data. Consumers are left with only the patchwork of state laws.

industries.industry: Big tech platforms (social networks, search engines, video services)
industries.note: The bill would force platforms to disclose opaque algorithms, offer a transparent-algorithm version of their feeds, ban manipulative dark patterns and child-directed autoplay, and open their behavioral experiments to informed consent and independent review boards. Their continued ability to profit from engagement-maximizing design is what the bill's protections exist to curb.

Brokers would have to register annually with the FTC, whose published list would make their industry visible for the first time. The penalties are light, but brokers profit from trading data people never knowingly gave up, so their interest runs against the bill's purpose.

Consent requirements for sensitive data and the data-minimization rule would sharply restrict the behavioral profiling and tracking that targeted advertising depends on. What adtech gains, consumers lose in privacy, and vice versa.

The bill creates approved certification programs and mandates privacy officers, privacy impact assessments, and internal controls—a new compliance market. These firms only profit if companies actually comply, so their interest runs with the public's.
Employee data is expressly excluded from covered data, leaving employers free to keep collecting and processing data about their own workers with none of the bill's rights or consent requirements.
